title: {{NAME}} and the Goal at the Edge of the Enchanted Pitch
moral: Believing in someone gives them the strength to believe in themselves.

pages.content:
The Enchanted Pitch lay in a clearing at the heart of the Silverwood, where the trees grew in perfect arches overhead and filtered the sunlight into a perpetual green-gold glow. Fireflies played among the grass blades even at noon. The goalposts were two ancient oak trunks whose branches had grown into natural crossbars over centuries of waiting. It was the most beautiful place {{NAME}} had ever kicked a ball.

It was also, today, the most urgent. The Silverwood Spring Festival came once a year, and tradition demanded a sunset match between the valley teams. But the Fernhill Strikers were missing their best midfielder: an Velociraptor named Bramble, who had arrived that morning and immediately sat down at the edge of the pitch and refused to move. Not from injury. Not from illness. From something quieter and harder to see.

Bramble was enormous. His green-scaled hide was the colour of deep river water, his thumb-spike claws rested on his knees, and his eyes, which were usually bright with the particular joy of a creature who loves the game, were dull and directed firmly at the ground. {{NAME}} had met this kind of stuck before, in other players, in younger teammates, sometimes in the mirror on bad days. It wasn't stubbornness. It was the particular paralysis of someone who had made one terrible mistake in the last match and couldn't see past it to today.

pages.content:
{{NAME}} sat beside Bramble on the grass. Not across from him, not standing over him. Beside him, at the same level, facing the same direction. For a full minute neither of them said anything, which felt at first uncomfortable and then surprisingly comfortable.

The silver unicorn appeared at the tree line without drama or announcement, as though she had simply always been there and {{NAME}} had only just noticed. She was called Mira, and she was the Silverwood's keeper, a role that meant different things depending on who needed her. She walked to Bramble with the unhurried gravity of someone arriving exactly on time and pressed her luminous horn very gently to the crown of his great head. She didn't speak. She just let her light fall over him, warm and patient.

Bramble let out a long, shuddering breath. The kind of breath that has been waiting a while to come out.

'Last match,' he said finally, in a voice like distant thunder trying to be quiet. 'I missed the cross. Easy ball. Everyone saw.' His thumb-spike traced a pattern in the grass. 'I keep seeing it.'

{{NAME}} thought for a moment. 'I've missed balls,' said {{NAME}}. 'Last Thursday. Really easy chip. In front of everyone.' Bramble turned his great head slowly. His eyes were brighter than before, just slightly, just enough. 'What did you do?' 'Came back the next day,' said {{NAME}}. Simple as that.

pages.content:
Bramble stood. He stood the way mountains stand: solidly, with the sense that this was where he was meant to be and had just temporarily forgotten.

When the match began at the golden hour, the Enchanted Pitch became the most alive place in the whole forest. The opposing team, the Ridge Runners, were three fleet Raptors and four human players, and they moved with coordinated speed that made them look like a single creature with many legs. The crowd that had gathered in the tree roots and on the broad branches above made sounds that dropped like warm rain.

Bramble played as though he were making something. Every pass deliberate, every position considered, his great body clearing space for the faster players around him with the calm generosity of someone who had remembered why they loved this. He set {{NAME}} up twice, perfectly weighted passes that asked nothing of the recipient except to run and receive.

The third time, {{NAME}} reversed it. Pushing wide, drawing two defenders, then cutting the ball back along the ground at exactly the pace Bramble's stride required, arriving at his left foot as though it had been sent by someone who believed completely in what would happen next. Bramble struck it. Clean. True. The ball curved past the Ridge Runners' goalkeeper with authority, hit the natural oak crossbar, and bounced in. The fireflies scattered upward in a glittering explosion of tiny lights.

pages.content:
The Ridge Runners equalised twelve minutes later with a goal that was frankly excellent and that the crowd appreciated even from the wrong side of it, which was the right response. The match sat at one-all and the light began its long, gorgeous decline toward sunset, painting everything amber and copper and something between them that had no name.

In the final minutes, with the shadows long and the fireflies growing brighter as the light dropped, the Enchanted Pitch seemed to hold its breath. {{NAME}} received the ball at midfield with two defenders closing. No clear pass. No clear shot. Only a moment and a decision.

Mira stepped from the tree line and stood at the edge of the pitch, her silver coat catching the last light and turning it into something older and calmer. She wasn't doing anything magical. She was just watching, with the particular attention of someone who believes in what they are seeing.

{{NAME}} played the pass instinctively, threading it through the impossible gap between the two defenders to Bramble, who was already there, already moving, already certain. His second goal of the match. The Silverwood erupted with the collective sound of every living thing in it expressing the same thing at the same time. Two-one. Final whistle. The fireflies rose in one great shimmering curtain above the ancient goalposts.

pages.content:
Afterward, the Silverwood settled into its evening self, the deep green dimming to a blue-tinged quiet, the fireflies thickening above the grass into something that looked almost like a second constellation.

Bramble sat at the edge of the pitch again, but the quality of the sitting was entirely different from the morning. His eyes were bright and directed outward, toward the trees, toward whatever was next. He had something in his expression that had not been there at sunrise. Mira stood nearby, her horn dimmed to its resting glow, doing nothing in particular except being present, which turned out to be everything.

'Thank you,' Bramble said to {{NAME}}, in his quiet thunder voice. 'For sitting beside me.' {{NAME}} shrugged, which was really a smile wearing a shrug as a coat. 'You did the hard part,' said {{NAME}} truthfully. 'I just stayed while you did it.'

The three of them sat together as the Silverwood breathed around them, ancient and patient and full of its own slow contentment. The fireflies performed their nightly ceremony overhead.

{{NAME}}'s eyes grew heavy as good earth growing its first seeds. Sleep now, gentle one. Let the Silverwood's quiet wrap around you like the greenest cloak. And wonder, in the softest part of your dreams, what game Mira herself played here before the oaks were old.
